pages.title: Pricing a design from its recipe

text.text: A florist loses money one stem at a time. Every design starts from a recipe, and the price comes from the recipe, not from a guess at the counter.
List every stem, every piece of greenery, the container and the extras: ribbon, foam, the care card. Look up each stem's
in Stems and cooler and add it up. That total goes on the order as
Fresh flowers are marked up three and a half times: the

column on each stem does that sum for you. Containers and hard goods are marked up two times. Labor is already inside the flower markup for everyday work; for sympathy and event pieces that take more than an hour, add a design fee.
on each order divides the flower and supply cost by the price. Keep it at
. The Pricing check marks anything over that.
When the customer names a price
Take the price without the delivery fee.
Divide by three and a half: that is what you may spend on flowers.
Build the recipe to that number, starting with the focal flowers, then filler and greens.
If they ask for peonies on a 65 USD budget, offer garden roses or ranunculus instead and say why.
Every stem that dies in the cooler is cost with no price. Keep
honest, buy twice a week instead of once, and use the oldest stems first in everyday work. Vase life tells you which stems to sell first: peonies and delphinium before eucalyptus and ruscus.

pages.title: A wedding, from consultation to load-in

text.text: Weddings are booked months ahead and judged in one afternoon. This is the order of work that keeps the money, the flowers and the timeline straight.
Use the Wedding consultation template on the event row. Ask for the budget before showing anything. Count every piece: bouquets, boutonnieres, ceremony arch, centerpieces per table. The
numbers drive the flower order later.
Send it within three days and move the event to
. Build it from recipes, exactly like a daily order, and keep the flower and rental cost under a third of the total. Rentals such as arches, urns and candles cost money too; put them in the cost.
A date is only held once 30% is paid. Press
on the row: it moves the event to Booked and stamps the date.
shows what is left; collect it two weeks before the wedding.
Three weeks out, confirm the final count with the couple or their planner.
Place the flower order with the wholesaler and the farm for delivery four days before the wedding, so blooms have time to open.
Processing day: strip, cut and hydrate every stem as it arrives.
Design day: bouquets last, the day before, kept cool.
Load-in: check the venue's timeline and the strike time. Photograph every piece in place.
. Collect rentals the next morning. Compare the real flower spend with the budget on the row; if a wedding ran over, the next proposal for that venue or that size should be priced higher.
